messages.content: I want to learn classifiers that reject shifting spurious cues without environment labels, but still preserve stable predictive features specific to minority groups. The goal also needs identifiability conditions and a concrete performance target.

The distinction is between a cue whose apparent usefulness changes under a shift and a feature whose predictive relationship remains stable, even if that feature is useful mainly within a minority group. Without environment labels, the classifier cannot simply be told which observations came from which environment. The identifiability question is therefore central: under what conditions could those two kinds of signal be distinguished from the available observations? The performance target is simultaneous improvement of at least 5 percentage points in worst-group accuracy over ERM, with no more than a 1-percentage-point loss in overall accuracy.
Does rejecting spurious cues mean treating every group-specific feature as suspect?

No. A feature can be specific to a minority group and still carry a stable predictive signal for that group. Rejecting it merely because its usefulness differs across groups would work against the goal. What matters is whether its predictive relationship is stable under the shifts of concern, not whether it is equally useful to every group. The intended classifier should avoid relying on shifting shortcuts while retaining stable information that helps predict outcomes for minority-group members.
Then what would make a shortcut identifiable as unstable rather than merely uncommon?

There must be some justified basis for distinguishing changes in its predictive relationship from changes in how often it appears. Conceptually, an unstable shortcut is one whose relationship to the target changes across relevant shifts; a stable minority-specific signal continues to predict within the minority group across those shifts. Rarity alone establishes neither property. The comparison needs enough relevant variation and common support to assess a relationship in comparable circumstances, rather than mistaking a change in group composition or feature frequency for a change in predictiveness.
Can you state the identifiability conditions more explicitly without assuming environment labels are supplied?

A defensible statement would make several conditions explicit. First, the observations or justified structural assumptions must contain enough information to distinguish relevant latent shifts, even though environment labels are not supplied. Second, stable candidates and shortcut candidates must not be perfectly inseparable in the available variation: there must be comparable cases or other justified structure that distinguishes their contributions. Third, the minority-specific signal must occur with enough support to assess its predictive relationship within that group. Fourth, the proposed distinction must be unique under the assumptions: a shifting-shortcut explanation and a stable-minority-signal explanation must not fit the available information equally well. These are conditions to specify and justify, not properties that can be presumed to hold.
Could you make the stability condition a little more precise?

As a conceptual formulation, let a candidate feature be assessed within a minority group across the relevant, possibly latent, regimes. On comparable feature values and with appropriate conditioning, its relationship to the target would remain the same across those regimes if it is a stable minority-specific signal, and it would provide predictive information within that group. A candidate shortcut would instead have a predictive relationship that changes across relevant regimes. This formulation does not make the regimes observable by itself; identifying or otherwise justifying the comparison remains part of the identifiability requirement.
Why emphasize comparable feature values?

Without overlap, apparent stability or instability can be impossible to distinguish from a lack of comparable observations. If a candidate appears only under one set of circumstances and another candidate only under a different set, their roles may be observationally confounded. An identifiability claim needs either adequate overlap for the comparison or an explicitly justified alternative assumption that supplies the missing distinction. Otherwise, calling one feature stable and the other spurious would go beyond what the observations establish.
And without environment labels, can I just infer the regimes and proceed?

Not automatically. Absence of environment labels does not rule out learning from variation in the observations, but it also does not guarantee that latent regimes can be recovered. Any proposal to use them needs conditions under which the relevant variation is detectable and the resulting distinction between feature roles is identifiable. Recovering a partition of observations would not, on its own, show that the partition corresponds to the shifts that matter for separating shortcuts from stable minority-specific signals.
So there may be cases where the two kinds of feature cannot be told apart?

Yes. If a shifting cue and a stable minority-specific feature always appear together in the information available for learning, and the assumptions provide no other way to separate their contributions, the distinction is not identifiable from that information. Both explanations could account for the same observations. The identifiability conditions should say what rules out that ambiguity, rather than promising to resolve it in every setting without environment labels.
How do I keep the minority-specific part from disappearing into an aggregate notion of stability?

State the stability requirement at the level where the signal matters. A feature need not be equally predictive for the majority to be worth preserving for a minority group. Looking only at an aggregate relationship could obscure a stable relationship within that minority group, particularly if the groups contribute differently to the aggregate. The goal calls for distinguishing that within-group stability from an unstable shortcut, not for requiring one universal feature relationship across all groups.
Does 'without environment labels' also mean I cannot use group labels anywhere?

The stated constraint concerns environment labels; it does not, by itself, specify whether group information is available during learning. Nor does it settle how groups are defined for evaluation. Those are separate questions that should not be silently answered one way or the other. What is fixed here is that the approach should not depend on supplied environment labels, while the identifiability account and the worst-group accuracy comparison must be clear about whatever group information they require.
Spell out the accuracy requirement against ERM.

The worst-group accuracy must be at least 5 percentage points higher than ERM’s worst-group accuracy. At the same time, overall accuracy must be no more than 1 percentage point lower than ERM’s overall accuracy; matching or exceeding ERM overall would also satisfy that second bound. These are percentage-point differences in accuracy, not relative percentage changes, and both comparisons have to hold together.
Is a gain for one selected minority group enough to meet the worst-group target?

Not necessarily. The target concerns worst-group accuracy: the minimum accuracy across the groups used for that evaluation. Improving one minority group would not meet the target if the resulting worst-group accuracy were still less than 5 percentage points above ERM’s worst-group accuracy. The group attaining the minimum could also differ between the classifiers. The comparison is between the two worst-group accuracy values, alongside the overall-accuracy constraint.
And good worst-group accuracy would prove that the classifier rejected shortcuts and preserved the right features?

The accuracy comparison would establish the stated performance target if both bounds were met, but it would not by itself prove why the classifier performed that way. The feature-level aim and the identifiability conditions address a different question: whether shifting spurious cues can be distinguished from stable minority-specific predictive information, and whether the classifier’s reliance reflects that distinction. It is important not to infer the mechanism solely from the two accuracy numbers.
Would it be accurate to frame all of this as a goal rather than an achieved result?

Yes. The aim is to learn such classifiers, specify the conditions under which the feature distinction is identifiable without environment labels, and attain the stated comparison with ERM. Nothing in that aim establishes that the conditions hold in a particular setting or that either accuracy threshold has already been reached.
One last distinction: if a cue sometimes predicts well, does calling it spurious mean it can never contain useful information?

No. A shifting spurious cue can be predictive in some circumstances. The concern is reliance on a relationship that does not remain dependable across the relevant shifts. Conversely, a minority-specific feature need not help every group to be worth keeping: its stable predictive value within the minority group is precisely what the goal seeks to preserve. The identifiability conditions need to make those two judgments distinguishable, rather than treating present-day predictiveness or group specificity alone as decisive.
For a concrete approach, could we train latent-subgroup invariant predictors using augmentations that vary shortcuts but preserve minority-specific signals?

Yes—that is the proposed approach. The augmentations would create variation in a suspected shortcut while leaving the stable predictive information, including information useful specifically to a minority group, intact. Training would then seek predictions that remain dependable across those variations, with the invariance framed around latent subgroups rather than requiring supplied environment labels. It is a proposal, not a claim that suitable augmentations or subgroups have already been identified.
What does “latent-subgroup invariant” add beyond ordinary invariance to augmented examples?

It keeps the minority-specific part of the goal in view. A broad requirement that every feature behave identically for everyone could suppress a stable signal that is useful within a minority group. Invariance within an appropriate latent subgroup instead asks whether predictions remain stable when a shortcut varies, without demanding that the same predictive features serve all groups equally. The subgroup is latent in the proposal; that term does not mean its membership is already known or correctly recoverable.
So the augmentation should change what the model might use as a shortcut, but not the information it ought to use?

Exactly. “Shortcut-varying, minority-signal-preserving” describes the intended distinction. If an augmentation changes only the suspected shifting cue, a predictor that relies heavily on that cue may change its prediction, while one relying on preserved stable information need not. But if the augmentation also damages a stable minority-specific signal, invariance to it could teach the wrong lesson. The preservation claim therefore has to be justified, not inferred merely from calling a transformation an augmentation.
Does the proposal assume we know which feature is the shortcut before training?

It does not state that the shortcut is known in advance. It does require a defensible way to produce variation that targets shortcut-like information while preserving minority-specific predictive information. Without such a distinction, the augmentation may not support the intended training signal. The proposal leaves open how that distinction would be made; it should not be read as a completed solution to the identifiability problem.
Could a useful minority signal itself look like a shortcut because it is not predictive for everyone?

Yes, which is why subgroup-specific stability matters. A feature’s usefulness being concentrated in a minority group does not by itself make it a shifting spurious cue. The relevant contrast is between a predictive relationship that remains stable for that group under the shifts of concern and one that changes with a shortcut. Augmentations must preserve the former even as they vary the latter.
How would invariance avoid washing out the minority signal?

The intended constraint is invariance to the shortcut changes introduced by the augmentations, not indifference to every difference between groups. If a minority-specific signal is preserved across augmented versions, the predictor can continue using it while becoming less sensitive to the varied shortcut. That is the rationale for pairing latent-subgroup invariance with minority-signal-preserving augmentations. Whether training actually achieves that separation remains to be established.
And “latent subgroup” is not just another name for an environment label?

No. An environment label would identify a supplied environment for an observation; the proposal does not require such labels. A latent subgroup is a grouping relevant to learning or assessing stable predictive behavior that is not simply given as an environment label. Calling it latent does not guarantee that it can be inferred, that it matches an evaluation group, or that it isolates the right signal. Those distinctions matter to the proposal’s feasibility.
If the inferred subgroup accidentally tracks a shortcut, would the invariance objective still help?

There would be no guarantee. A grouping driven by the shortcut could make the proposed invariance miss the intended stable minority-specific relationship, or reinforce an unhelpful distinction. The proposal depends on the latent-subgroup framing and the augmentations being informative about the shortcut-versus-stable-signal distinction. That dependence is another reason to state identifiability conditions rather than assume the labels’ absence is harmless.
What conditions would be especially relevant to this particular proposal?

At a conceptual level, the shortcut must be capable of varying in the proposed augmented comparisons while the target-relevant minority signal remains available. The transformations must preserve the meaning of the prediction problem, rather than create contradictory examples. There must also be enough information to distinguish stability within a relevant minority subgroup from apparent stability caused by inseparable features or inadequate overlap. Finally, the latent subgroup used for invariance must be distinguishable in a way that serves that comparison; otherwise, multiple shortcut and stable-signal explanations could remain equally compatible with what training observes. These are requirements to justify, not established properties of a particular augmentation scheme.
Is it fair to say augmentation supplies a substitute for missing environment labels?

It is fairer to say the proposal uses controlled variation from augmentations to pursue invariance without relying on supplied environment labels. An augmentation is not automatically equivalent to observing a real environment shift. Its usefulness depends on whether it varies the shortcuts that matter while preserving the stable signals that matter, especially for minority groups. Merely producing different-looking inputs would not establish that.
What if changing a suspected shortcut also changes a stable minority-specific feature?

Then that augmentation would not satisfy the proposed minority-signal-preserving condition. Enforcing invariance across it could penalize reliance on precisely the information the classifier should retain. The proposal calls for shortcut-varying and minority-signal-preserving augmentations together; satisfying only the first half would not express its intended mechanism.
Conversely, what if an augmentation preserves everything the predictor currently uses?

If it does not vary the shortcut the predictor relies on, invariance across that augmentation provides little basis for discouraging that reliance. The proposed training signal needs meaningful shortcut variation, not variation in name only. The two parts of the augmentation description have different roles: one challenges shortcut dependence, and the other protects stable minority-specific predictive information.
I want the performance target to remain explicit. How should it be stated here?

The target is a gain of at least 5 percentage points in worst-group accuracy over ERM, while overall accuracy is at most 1 percentage point below ERM’s overall accuracy. Both are comparisons with ERM, and both must hold for the target to be met. The proposal aims for that outcome; it does not report that the gain or the overall-accuracy bound has been achieved.
Would a large worst-group improvement be enough if overall accuracy dropped by more than 1 point?

No. Even a worst-group improvement of at least 5 percentage points would not meet the stated target if overall accuracy fell by more than 1 percentage point relative to ERM. Likewise, keeping overall accuracy within the bound would not compensate for a worst-group gain smaller than 5 percentage points. The aim is to satisfy both comparisons simultaneously.
Is the worst-group gain about whichever group the proposed classifier helps most?

No. It compares worst-group accuracy—the minimum across the groups used in evaluation—for the proposed classifier against ERM’s worst-group accuracy. A gain for a favored group is not sufficient if the minimum accuracy does not improve by at least 5 percentage points. The proposed focus on preserving minority-specific signals is meant to help avoid sacrificing groups whose stable predictors differ from those dominant in the aggregate, but that motivation is not itself a measured gain.
Can we say the invariant predictor will reject shifting cues if the augmentations meet their description?

That is the intended training pressure, but “will reject” would be too strong without further conditions. The augmentations would need to expose consequential shortcut variation, preserve the minority signal, and be used in a way that makes shortcut-insensitive predictions attainable without losing useful information. Even then, the behavior of a trained classifier is a separate matter to assess. The proposal describes a route toward rejecting shifting spurious cues, not a guarantee by definition.
Then give me a compact formulation that keeps both the method and its limits clear.

Propose training latent-subgroup invariant predictors with augmentations designed to vary shifting shortcuts while preserving stable minority-specific predictive signals, without requiring environment labels. The intended outcome is at least a 5-percentage-point gain in worst-group accuracy over ERM with no more than a 1-percentage-point loss in overall accuracy. The approach depends on justifying that the augmentations and latent-subgroup comparisons can distinguish unstable shortcuts from stable minority-specific signals; neither that distinction nor the performance target is established merely by stating the proposal.
What observable augmentation-consistency and subgroup-support conditions would distinguish shifting shortcuts from stable minority-specific cues without environment labels?

The key is to separate what can be checked in augmented observations from what those checks would justify. One candidate condition is that an augmentation measurably varies a suspected shortcut while leaving the prediction target and the candidate minority-specific signal intact. Another is that, within a sufficiently supported subgroup, the signal remains predictive across those augmented comparisons while dependence on the shortcut does not remain dependable. Those observations could support the distinction, but only if the augmentations genuinely represent the relevant shortcut variation and the subgroup comparisons are identifiable. Consistency alone does not certify either point.
What exactly would be observable about augmentation consistency?

For paired original and augmented observations, one could ask whether the candidate signal remains present, whether the suspected shortcut changes, and whether the target is appropriately preserved. One could also examine whether predictions stay consistent across the pair. These are different observations: a model’s consistent predictions do not prove that the augmentation preserved a stable signal, and a visibly changed cue does not prove that it is a shortcut. The proposed distinction needs evidence about what the transformation changes and preserves, not just a prediction-agreement score.
Would prediction agreement across augmentations be the invariance condition?

It could be an observable expression of invariance, but it is not sufficient by itself. A predictor that ignores all informative features might also agree with itself across augmentations. For the agreement to be meaningful here, the predictions must remain tied to predictive information retained by the augmentation, including information useful within a minority subgroup. Otherwise, consistency could reflect a loss of useful sensitivity rather than successful rejection of a shifting shortcut.
And if predictions change when the supposed shortcut changes?

That would indicate sensitivity to the augmentation, but it would not by itself identify the cause. The transformation might also have changed a stable cue or altered the meaning of the observation. To interpret prediction changes as shortcut dependence, the comparison needs a credible preservation condition: the target-relevant information being protected must remain comparable while the suspected shortcut varies.
How does subgroup support enter the argument?

A claim that a cue is stable and predictive specifically within a minority subgroup needs enough observations of that subgroup, including informative comparisons across the relevant augmented variations. If the cue appears too rarely, or only together with the suspected shortcut, its contribution cannot be separated reliably from the shortcut’s. Support is therefore about more than subgroup size: it also concerns overlap and variation sufficient to compare the cues without treating one inseparable pattern as evidence for two different explanations.
Do we need the minority-specific cue to appear outside the minority subgroup for that overlap?

Not necessarily. A cue can be specific to a minority subgroup and still be assessed for stability within that subgroup. What is needed is relevant support for the within-subgroup comparison: the protected cue remains available while the suspected shortcut can vary, or some other justified structure distinguishes their contributions. Requiring the cue to be equally present or equally predictive outside the subgroup would change the question rather than resolve it.
Could the subgroup itself be defined by the suspected shortcut?

That would be a concern. If subgroup membership simply tracks the shortcut, a within-subgroup consistency check may conceal the very variation needed to test shortcut dependence. An observable subgroup-support condition should therefore address whether the proposed subgroup admits comparisons that separate shortcut variation from the stable cue. It should not assume that a discovered grouping is appropriate merely because it has a name or contains enough observations.
But with no environment labels, how can we tell whether augmentation variation stands in for the shifts we care about?

We cannot tell from the absence of labels alone. An augmentation offers an observable comparison, not automatic evidence about every relevant shift. The condition would have to say why its changes are informative about a shifting shortcut and why the minority-specific predictive signal survives those changes. If that connection cannot be justified, augmentation consistency establishes only consistency under the chosen transformations, not stability under otherwise unidentified shifts.
Suppose the shortcut and minority cue always move together in the observations. What does the condition say then?

Unless an augmentation or another justified source of variation separates them while preserving the relevant target information, the distinction is not identifiable from those observations. The same apparent predictive behavior could be attributed to either cue. A useful condition should acknowledge that limit explicitly rather than labeling one cue stable and the other spurious without a separating comparison.
Is there a risk that requiring consistency will erase a real minority-specific difference?

Yes, if consistency is demanded across changes that remove or alter the minority-specific signal, or if it is interpreted as requiring identical feature relationships for every group. The relevant condition is narrower: predictions should remain consistent when the shortcut varies and the stable, target-relevant minority cue is preserved. Genuine predictive differences associated with that preserved cue need not be suppressed.
So how should I phrase the two kinds of observable condition side by side?

You could ask whether augmented comparisons exhibit **selective variation**—the suspected shortcut changes while the target and candidate minority-specific cue remain meaningfully comparable—and whether there is **subgroup support**—enough within-subgroup variation and overlap to assess the cue’s predictive relationship separately from the shortcut. Prediction consistency across those comparisons can then be examined as a consequence. The wording should make clear that selective variation and support require justification; observed agreement alone cannot establish them.
Would those conditions be sufficient to identify the distinction?

Not without a further uniqueness condition. Even with apparently selective augmentations and adequate support, there must not be an equally compatible explanation in which the roles of the cues differ. In particular, the observable comparisons need to discriminate between a cue whose predictive relationship changes under relevant variation and one that remains predictive within the minority subgroup. If both explanations fit the same observations, the distinction remains unresolved without environment labels or additional justified assumptions.
Can this be expressed without claiming that the latent subgroups are already known?

Yes. Phrase it as a question about candidate or inferred subgroups: is there sufficient, non-circular support within a relevant subgroup to compare preserved predictive information across shortcut-varying augmentations? Then ask what assumptions make that subgroup and the cue distinction identifiable. This keeps the conditions open for investigation rather than treating latent subgroup membership, augmentation validity, or the shortcut–signal separation as established facts.

Here is a hypothesis about the conditions we were discussing: with label overlap and two independent shortcut interventions per subgroup, stable minority cues retain conditional label association, while shortcut associations vanish.

That frames a possible way to distinguish the two kinds of cue without environment labels. Label overlap would make within-subgroup comparisons of label association possible. The two independent shortcut interventions per subgroup would provide variation directed at shortcuts. Under the hypothesis, a stable minority cue remains conditionally associated with the label across those comparisons, whereas an association attributable to a shifting shortcut vanishes. This is an expected distinction under the stated conditions, not an observed result.
What does label overlap contribute that an intervention alone would not?

Label overlap means the relevant subgroup comparisons contain the label variation needed to examine an association. If a subgroup comparison effectively contains only one label value, a cue’s conditional relationship to the label cannot be distinguished there in the intended way. Intervening on a shortcut may change that cue, but without label overlap it would not by itself establish whether a minority-specific cue retains conditional label association.
Is the label overlap meant to hold within each subgroup?

Yes. Because the hypothesis makes a claim per subgroup and aims to preserve minority-specific signals, overlap needs to support the relevant comparisons within each subgroup. Overlap only in the aggregate could conceal a lack of label variation in a particular subgroup. The hypothesis does not say that a cue must have the same association in all subgroups.
Why specify two independent shortcut interventions per subgroup rather than just shortcut variation in general?

The hypothesis specifically relies on two independent shortcut interventions for each subgroup. Conceptually, two distinct sources of shortcut-directed variation offer a stronger check than observing a single change: an apparent pattern tied to one intervention alone need not persist under the other. Independence is important to the proposed distinction because duplicating the same shortcut change would not provide the same separate comparison. That rationale does not, on its own, prove that two interventions are sufficient.
Does independent mean they have to affect two different shortcuts?

Not necessarily. The statement requires two independent shortcut interventions per subgroup; it does not say they must target different shortcuts. The essential claim is that they furnish independent shortcut-directed comparisons. How independence is defined and justified would matter before using the hypothesis as an identification argument, but it should not be silently replaced by a requirement about the number of distinct shortcut features.
When you say the stable cue retains a conditional label association, what is being held conditional?

The intended claim is that, in appropriate within-subgroup comparisons that account for the intervention context, the stable minority cue remains associated with the label. The conditioning has to permit like-for-like comparisons rather than turn a change in subgroup composition or shortcut prevalence into an apparent change in the cue’s relationship. The hypothesis does not fix a full set of conditioning variables, so it is better not to assert a particular formula as though it were already established.
Does “retains” mean the minority cue must predict equally well for the majority?

No. Retaining conditional label association is a within-subgroup statement. A cue can carry stable predictive information for a minority subgroup without being comparably useful for the majority. The hypothesis is meant to preserve that distinction rather than treat group-specific usefulness as evidence that a cue is a shifting shortcut.
What exactly vanishes for a shortcut?

The hypothesis says shortcut associations with the label vanish under the stated comparisons. It does not say the shortcut feature disappears from the observations, or that it was never associated with the label before the interventions. The contrast is between a stable minority cue’s retained conditional label association and an association attributable to a shifting shortcut that does not survive the independent shortcut interventions.
Could a shortcut still appear predictive in an unconditioned aggregate?

That would not contradict the proposed contrast. An aggregate association can differ from a conditional, within-subgroup association assessed through shortcut interventions. The hypothesis concerns what happens to the shortcut association in the relevant conditional comparisons, not a promise that every possible aggregate association becomes zero.
If a cue stays associated with the label after only one intervention, should we call it stable?

Not on the basis of this hypothesis. It specifies label overlap and two independent shortcut interventions per subgroup. Persistence under only one could reflect something particular to that comparison. Even persistence under both would need the interventions and the within-subgroup comparisons to satisfy the conditions being claimed; the observed pattern should not automatically be promoted to proof of stability.
Could an intervention accidentally damage the minority cue?

Yes, and then the proposed contrast would be hard to interpret. A shortcut intervention used for this purpose must allow the stable minority cue’s conditional label association to be assessed, rather than destroying the cue or changing the prediction problem in an unaccounted-for way. If a minority cue loses its association because the intervention altered it, that loss would not establish that it was a shortcut.
And what if the shortcut and stable cue cannot be varied separately?

Then even two nominal interventions might not distinguish their roles. If every shortcut change also changes the candidate stable cue in an inseparable way, the conditional associations could be ambiguous. The hypothesis needs independent, informative shortcut interventions and sufficient within-subgroup support; merely counting two interventions would not resolve confounding between the cues.
Do the interventions supply environment labels indirectly?

They supply comparisons based on the interventions, not supplied labels for naturally occurring environments. The hypothesis is a possible answer to how one might distinguish cues without environment labels: use label overlap and independent shortcut-directed variation within each subgroup. Whether those comparisons capture the shifting shortcuts of interest is part of what would have to be justified.
Does the hypothesis identify latent subgroups as well as features?

It states the proposed conditions per subgroup, but it does not by itself explain how latent subgroups are found or establish that any inferred grouping is the right one. To apply the contrast, each relevant subgroup would need enough label overlap and both independent shortcut interventions to support its comparisons. A grouping that merely follows the shortcut could undermine the intended distinction.
Can you restate the testable contrast without turning the hypothesis into a finding?

The hypothesized contrast is: given label overlap and two independent shortcut interventions within each subgroup, examine conditional associations with the label across those comparisons. Stable minority-specific cues are expected to retain their conditional association; associations due to shifting shortcuts are expected to vanish. The question is whether the stated conditions genuinely hold and whether that contrast appears—not whether it has already been demonstrated.
So the number and placement of the interventions are part of the claim, not optional details?

Right. It says **two independent shortcut interventions per subgroup**, together with **label overlap**. Replacing them with one intervention, two non-independent versions of the same comparison, or interventions available only in the aggregate would change the hypothesis. The expected retained-versus-vanishing conditional associations are tied to those stated conditions.
For Waterbirds, I’d like to cross background-scene swaps with independent palette edits, then check label overlap and conditional cue–label stability in inferred subgroups.

That is a plan for making the proposed distinctions observable. Crossing the two augmentation types means examining background-scene swaps alongside independently applied palette edits, including their combined variation, rather than relying on just one kind of change. The checks would then ask whether inferred subgroups have the label overlap needed for comparison and whether candidate cues retain their conditional relationships with the label across the augmented comparisons. The plan does not yet establish that either augmentation changes only a shortcut or preserves every signal of interest.
What is gained by crossing the swaps and edits instead of looking at them separately?

The cross lets you ask whether an apparent cue–label relationship is consistent across variation in both dimensions, including when they vary together. A relationship that looks stable under a background-scene swap alone might behave differently when palette is also edited, or vice versa. That makes the comparisons more informative, provided the combined changes remain interpretable. It does not, by itself, prove that the two changes isolate particular cues.
Does “independent palette edits” mean we can assume palette has no connection to the background-scene swaps?

It describes palette edits as an independently applied augmentation axis, rather than an edit determined by the chosen background-scene swap. That independence in how the changes are applied should not be confused with a guarantee that their effects on candidate cues are separable. The checks still need to consider whether an edit changes information that was supposed to remain available.
What would label overlap mean in this plan?

It means that an inferred subgroup contains the relevant label variation for assessing a cue’s relationship to the label in the intended comparisons. If a subgroup provides no meaningful comparison between label values, a conditional cue–label association there cannot be interpreted in the way the plan requires. The overlap check belongs within inferred subgroups, rather than being satisfied merely because labels vary across Waterbirds as a whole.
Should overlap be checked before looking at cue–label stability?

Conceptually, yes: overlap is a prerequisite for interpreting the subgroup-level stability check. If the needed comparisons lack support, an apparent stable or unstable association could reflect that limitation rather than a property of the cue. This is a logical ordering of the checks, not a claim that either check has already been performed.
When you say “conditional cue–label stability,” what is being compared?

Within an inferred subgroup, the question is whether a candidate cue’s association with the label remains comparable across the background-scene swaps and independently applied palette edits, including their crossed comparisons. “Conditional” signals that the association is assessed in comparable circumstances rather than inferred from an aggregate pattern that might change with subgroup composition. The plan does not specify a particular conditioning formula, so it would be premature to treat one as fixed.
Would a cue count as stable merely because its frequency does not change after augmentation?

No. Frequency and conditional association with the label are different things. A cue might appear at the same rate but become less informative about the label, or its frequency might change while its within-subgroup label relationship remains comparable. The proposed check concerns the latter relationship; examining what the augmentations actually change helps determine whether that relationship can be interpreted.
What if the predictions are consistent across every crossed augmentation?

That would describe prediction behavior, but the planned check is also about candidate cues and their conditional associations with labels. Prediction consistency alone would not show that a useful minority-specific cue was preserved, or that the varied information was a shifting shortcut. The label-overlap and cue–label checks help keep those questions separate.
Do inferred subgroups introduce a risk of circular reasoning?

They can. If an inferred subgroup is defined in a way that effectively builds in the association being tested, observing that association within it may be uninformative. Likewise, if subgroup assignment changes merely because the augmentation changes a candidate shortcut, a comparison described as within-subgroup may no longer compare like with like. The plan therefore calls for checking support and interpreting stability in inferred subgroups carefully, not assuming that inference alone makes them suitable.
Would it be enough to have label overlap somewhere among the inferred subgroups?

Not for a claim about a particular subgroup. The overlap must support the conditional comparison wherever that comparison is made. An inferred subgroup without the needed label variation cannot inherit support from another subgroup. The plan calls for checking label overlap in inferred subgroups, so a pooled overlap figure would not answer the entire question.
Can the combined swap and palette edit create a problem even if each change looks interpretable on its own?

Yes, that is a possibility to examine rather than assume away. Crossing the changes could affect a candidate cue or the meaning of an observation differently from either change alone. A stability comparison under the combined augmentation is informative only if the resulting observations still support the intended label and cue comparisons. The plan specifies the cross; it does not declare that every crossed example will pass that interpretability check.
Are background-scene swaps and palette edits already established as shortcut interventions on Waterbirds?

Not by this plan. They are the two augmentation types proposed for the Waterbirds checks. Whether they create the relevant shortcut variation, and whether they preserve any stable minority-specific cue being assessed, are questions to examine. Naming the transformations does not settle their effects.
How would I phrase a negative outcome without overinterpreting it?

If a proposed within-subgroup comparison lacks label overlap, you could say that the conditional association is not assessable from that comparison. If an association differs across augmentations, you could report that lack of observed stability while keeping open whether the cue changed, the subgroup comparison changed, or the augmentation affected other relevant information. Those descriptions do not automatically identify a shortcut or refute the possibility of a stable minority-specific cue.
And if a cue does retain its conditional association across the crossed changes?

That would be evidence of stability under those particular, interpretable augmented comparisons, assuming sufficient label overlap and appropriate within-subgroup support. It would not automatically establish stability under every possible shift or prove that the inferred subgroup is the uniquely correct one. The scope of the observation should remain tied to what the background-scene swaps and independent palette edits actually vary.
So the plan is about testing the quality of the comparisons as well as the cue associations?

Yes. On Waterbirds, cross background-scene swaps with independent palette edits, then examine whether the inferred subgroups support label comparisons and whether candidate cues show conditional cue–label stability across those comparisons. Interpreting the result also requires attention to what the augmentations preserve and change. Those are planned checks, not findings about overlap, subgroup validity, or which cues are stable.

Let’s make the Waterbirds activity concrete: create crossed scene-swap and palette-edit views, then test label overlap and subgroup-conditional label associations for background, palette, and morphology.

The activity has two parts. First, create Waterbirds views that cross background-scene swaps with palette edits, so the comparisons include variation along both augmentation axes. Then, within inferred subgroups, check whether there is label overlap and assess the conditional association of each named cue—background, palette, and morphology—with the label. This specifies what to create and test; it does not state what those tests will find.
Why test all three cues instead of just checking whether predictions stay the same?
